children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Vital signs from a camera covers the estimation of pulse, breathing rate, and sometimes blood oxygen or blood pressure using ordinary video from a phone, laptop, or webcam rather than a contact sensor.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care covers the continuous or near continuous physiological measurements collected by consumer and medical grade devices, including heart rate, heart rhythm, oxygen saturation, sleep stages, step counts, skin temperature and glucose levels.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care covers the use of chat interfaces and voice agents to gather symptoms, offer initial guidance, and route patients to the right level of care.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health cover the passive and active data that phones, wearables and keyboards produce which may relate to mood, sleep, activity and social contact.

sections.body: Telemedicine and triage is the part of clinical artificial intelligence that sits between a person and a clinician, deciding who needs care, how soon, and what can be measured without a clinic visit. In practice, symptom checkers ask structured questions and return an urgency band, video visits run face and chest motion through models that estimate pulse and breathing rate, and consumer wearables feed heart rhythm, sleep and activity data into review workflows. Conversational systems handle intake, follow-up and routine coaching, and language models scan text for signals associated with low mood or crisis. The work is operational rather than speculative: routing queues, flagging deterioration, and filling gaps where a clinician is not physically present.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Triage accuracy is uneven. Systems perform reasonably on common presentations and poorly on rare or overlapping ones, and they inherit the biases of the data they were trained on, which shows up in unequal error rates across groups. Camera vital signs work under good light and stillness and degrade with motion, skin tone variation and poor bandwidth, so they are used as screening aids rather than replacements for a cuff or a pulse oximeter. Wearable data is abundant but noisy, and the evidence that it changes outcomes is thinner than its adoption suggests. Conversational care is bounded by its inability to examine, and mental health signal detection raises real problems of false positives, consent and escalation when no one is available to respond. Nothing here diagnoses on its own, and the honest position is that these tools assist a clinical process that still carries the responsibility.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section moves from first contact to measurement to ongoing monitoring to conversation to the most sensitive signals. Symptom Triage and Routing covers the entry point, the question sets and urgency logic that decide where a patient goes next. Vital Signs from a Camera explains what contactless measurement can and cannot recover from a video frame, which matters for anyone judging remote exams. Wearable Data in Clinical Care follows the stream after the visit, covering how device data is filtered, interpreted and acted on between appointments. Conversational Care and Its Limits examines dialogue systems for intake and coaching and where they break down, and Digital Signals of Mental Health addresses text and behaviour based detection, its false positives and the ethics of acting on them. Read together they trace a single patient journey, and read separately each answers a narrower question about what the technology is actually doing at that step.
